Analysis of Regular Statistical Models

Introduction¶

We will now analyse the special case when the true distribution is regular for the statistical model. This covers the classical Bayesian statistics. We analyse the regular posterior distribution, and observe the universal structure that is the asymptotic behavior of this distribution. The theorem is akin to central limit theorem, called the Bayesian central limit theorem / Bernstein–von Mises theorem. We also look at the expansions of the observables in this special case. We finally introduce point estimators, and with this, we cover the conventional asymptotic theory and the basic Bayesian treatment.

This part is more intensive than the previous parts, we are reaching the deep parts of the subject slowly. It is recommended to read the writeup on primer probability and Laplace method before moving ahead.

Observe below that we have already forgone realizability, a major assumption that need not hold in the singular models of our interest (such as the neural networks we use in practice).

The 1-D example¶

Our first goal is to estimate the partition function, which is a Laplace integral. We will first start with a simpler example, and we will build and motivate our solution from this method. Once the method is understood, it is all about the control.

Theorem: Let h∈C3[α,β]h \in C^3[\alpha, \beta]h∈C3[α,β] have a unique minimum w0w_0w0​ in the interior. Let H=h′′(w0)>0H = h''(w_0) > 0H=h′′(w0​)>0. Let φ∈C1\varphi \in C^1φ∈C1, φ(w0)>0\varphi(w_0) > 0φ(w0​)>0. Then

I(n)=∫αβe−nhφdw∼e−nh(w0)φ(w0)2πnHI(n) = \int_\alpha^\beta e^{-nh}\varphi dw \sim e^{-nh(w_0)}\varphi(w_0)\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{nH}}I(n)=∫αβ​e−nhφdw∼e−nh(w0​)φ(w0​)nH2π​​
(1)

(Warning: Do not worry about all the analytical assumptions too much just now, you will add them yourself as you go through the proof)

Proof:

We first centre the integral.

I(n)=e−nh(w0)∫αβe−n(h(w)−h(w0))φ(w)dwI(n) = e^{-nh(w_0)}\int_\alpha^\beta e^{-n(h(w) - h(w_0))}\varphi(w) dwI(n)=e−nh(w0​)∫αβ​e−n(h(w)−h(w0​))φ(w)dw
(2)

Now we do a Taylor expansion of the exponent of the exponential, as Laplace method dictates. Recall that according to the method, we must split the integral into two parts. The first part will be over the set where most of the mass is concentrated (it is clear that this is some neighborhood of w0w_0w0​) and we must show that the second integral is negligible compared to the first one, typically by looking at the fraction. The control is in choosing the right neighborhood. Also recall that we estimate the neighborhood integral by sandwiching. Let us do this now.

h(w)−h(w0)=Δh′(w0)+12h′′(w0)Δ2+16h′′′(c)Δ3h(w) - h(w_0) = \Delta h'(w_0) + \frac{1}{2}h''(w_0)\Delta^2 + \frac{1}{6}h'''(c)\Delta^3h(w)−h(w0​)=Δh′(w0​)+21​h′′(w0​)Δ2+61​h′′′(c)Δ3
(3)

This is the Taylor expansion with the Lagrange remainder. Δ=w−w0\Delta = w - w_0Δ=w−w0​, and c∈[α,β]c \in [\alpha, \beta]c∈[α,β], which is the parameter space for this case.

The idea is here that we really want to be integrating only the first two terms, as we can handle that. So we want the third one to be negligible. Thus we want to naturally choose a neighborhood around w0w_0w0​ of radius δn\delta_nδn​ (dependent on nnn because we want to zero in on where the mass of the function is as nnn increases, so we must decrease the neighborhood accordingly), A={w:0≤∣∣w−w0∣∣<δn}A = \{w: 0 \leq ||w - w_0|| < \delta_n\}A={w:0≤∣∣w−w0​∣∣<δn​}, and in this set, ∣∣Δ∣∣≤δn||\Delta|| \leq \delta_n∣∣Δ∣∣≤δn​, hence we get the first control that we want: nδn3→0n \delta_n^3 \to 0nδn3​→0.

Let us estimate the integral on this set. First of all, observe that the third Taylor term, which we now call Rn(w)R_n(w)Rn​(w), satisfies ∣Rn(w)∣≤Mδn3|R_n(w)| \leq M\delta_n^3∣Rn​(w)∣≤Mδn3​ (Observe that AAA is compact and the third derivative of hhh is continuous) On this note, we call the first term and the second term A1A_1A1​ and A2A_2A2​ respectively.

IA(n)=e−nh(w0)∫Ae−nA1−nA2−nRn(w)φ(w)dwI_A(n) = e^{-nh(w_0)}\int_Ae^{-nA_1 - nA_2 - nR_n(w)}\varphi(w) dwIA​(n)=e−nh(w0​)∫A​e−nA1​−nA2​−nRn​(w)φ(w)dw
(4)

Also, since φ\varphiφ is C1C^1C1 on a compact interval, we can write

φ(w)=φ(w0)+φ′(c)(w−w0)≤φ(w0)+aδn\varphi(w) = \varphi(w_0) + \varphi'(c)(w - w_0) \leq \varphi(w_0) + a\delta_nφ(w)=φ(w0​)+φ′(c)(w−w0​)≤φ(w0​)+aδn​
(5)

for some constant aaa.

Hence, we can now sandwich and estimate the integral.

exp⁡(−nh(w0)−nMδn3)(φ(w0)−aδn)G≤IA(n)\exp(-nh(w_0) - nM\delta_n^3)(\varphi(w_0) - a\delta_n)G\leq I_A(n)exp(−nh(w0​)−nMδn3​)(φ(w0​)−aδn​)G≤IA​(n)
(6)

IA(n)≤exp⁡(−nh(w0)+nMδn3)(φ(w0)+aδn)GI_A(n)\leq \exp(-nh(w_0) + nM\delta_n^3)(\varphi(w_0) + a\delta_n) GIA​(n)≤exp(−nh(w0​)+nMδn3​)(φ(w0​)+aδn​)G

where GGG is the leftover integral.

Since nδn3→0n\delta_n^3 \to 0nδn3​→0 and δn→0\delta_n \to 0δn​→0, the prefactors e±nMδn3e^{\pm nM\delta_n^3}e±nMδn3​ tend to 1 and φ(w0)±aδn\varphi(w_0) \pm a\delta_nφ(w0​)±aδn​ tend to φ(w0)\varphi(w_0)φ(w0​). Dividing the sandwich through, we get, as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞,

IA(n)exp⁡(−nh(w0))φ(w0)Gn→1\frac{I_A(n)}{\exp(-nh(w_0))\varphi(w_0)G_n} \to 1exp(−nh(w0​))φ(w0​)Gn​IA​(n)​→1
(8)

Let us calculate the integral and be over with it. Actually, to compute the integral, we would actually have to complete the square and then use the Gaussian integral formula, but we are in good luck since A1=0A_1 = 0A1​=0, since w0w_0w0​ is the minimum. But still keep the method in mind, it will come in use later.

Thus, we can do a simple change of variable to get

Gn=∫Ae−nH(w−w0)2/2dw=1nH∫−nHδnnHδne−t2/2dtG_n = \int_A e^{-nH(w-w_0)^2/2}dw = \sqrt{\frac{1}{nH}}\int_{-\sqrt{nH}\delta_n}^{\sqrt{nH}\delta_n}e^{-t^2/2}dtGn​=∫A​e−nH(w−w0​)2/2dw=nH1​​∫−nH​δn​nH​δn​​e−t2/2dt
(9)

We can choose δn\delta_nδn​ such that nδn→∞\sqrt{n}\delta_n \to \inftyn​δn​→∞ as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞ (this is not contradicting the previous control). Hence Gn∼2πnHG_n \sim \sqrt{\dfrac{2\pi}{nH}}Gn​∼nH2π​​. Hence, our estimate of the integral is

IA(n)∼exp⁡(−nh(w0))φ(w0)2πnHI_A(n) \sim \exp(-nh(w_0))\varphi(w_0)\sqrt{\dfrac{2\pi}{nH}}IA​(n)∼exp(−nh(w0​))φ(w0​)nH2π​​
(10)

Now we need to show that the second integral is negligible, that is IB(n)/IA(n)→0I_B(n)/I_A(n) \to 0IB​(n)/IA​(n)→0, where B=W/AB = W / AB=W/A.

This involves finding a lower bound for h(w)−h(w0)h(w) - h(w_0)h(w)−h(w0​). This will upper bound our integrand, which is what we want.

Let us write the Taylor expansion again.

h(w)−h(w0)=12h′′(w0)Δ2+16h′′′(c)Δ3h(w) - h(w_0) = \frac{1}{2}h''(w_0)\Delta^2 + \frac{1}{6}h'''(c)\Delta^3h(w)−h(w0​)=21​h′′(w0​)Δ2+61​h′′′(c)Δ3

The idea is that even though we know that the second order term is positive (assumption), the third order term can be negative, and hence it is not straightforward to lower bound this. However, if we can upper bound the norm of the third order term, we can do this. The idea is that it is less than any given factor of the second order term (say half).

Claim: For all www with ∣Δ∣=∣w−w0∣≤η|\Delta| = |w - w_0| \leq \eta∣Δ∣=∣w−w0​∣≤η, for a suitable η>0\eta > 0η>0 chosen below,

where the last inequality needs Mη6≤H4\dfrac{M\eta}{6} \leq \dfrac{H}{4}6Mη​≤4H​. This gives our reverse engineering choice of η=3H2M\eta = \dfrac{3H}{2M}η=2M3H​, in which case the claim is true. Hence on B1B_1B1​, h(w)−h(w0)≥12HΔ2−14HΔ2=14HΔ2≥14Hδn2h(w) - h(w_0) \geq \frac{1}{2}H\Delta^2 - \frac{1}{4}H\Delta^2 = \frac{1}{4}H\Delta^2 \geq \frac{1}{4}H\delta_n^2h(w)−h(w0​)≥21​HΔ2−41​HΔ2=41​HΔ2≥41​Hδn2​.

What happens on B2B_2B2​ with this choice of η\etaη?

Observe that B2B_2B2​ is a compact set, hence since h(w)h(w)h(w) is a continuous function and w0w_0w0​ is the unique minimum, for all w∈B2w \in B_2w∈B2​, h(w)−h(w0)≥mη>0h(w) - h(w_0) \geq m_\eta > 0h(w)−h(w0​)≥mη​>0 where the minimum is achieved. h(w)−h(w0)≥14h′′(w0)δn2h(w) - h(w_0) \geq \frac{1}{4}h''(w_0)\delta_n^2h(w)−h(w0​)≥41​h′′(w0​)δn2​

The same is true for w∈B1w \in B_1w∈B1​ by the previous argument, hence it holds on all of BBB. Now let us bound the integrand. Since we have

IB(n)=e−nh(w0)∫Be−n(h(w)−h(w0))φ(w)dwI_B(n) = e^{-nh(w_0)}\int_Be^{-n(h(w) - h(w_0))}\varphi(w)dwIB​(n)=e−nh(w0​)∫B​e−n(h(w)−h(w0​))φ(w)dw

we get,

0≤IB(n)≤ce−nh(w0)e−n4Hδn20 \leq I_B(n) \leq ce^{-nh(w_0)}e^{-\frac{n}{4}H\delta_n^2}0≤IB​(n)≤ce−nh(w0​)e−4n​Hδn2​

IB(n)IA(n)≤ce−nH4δn2n\frac{I_B(n)}{I_A(n)} \leq c {e^{-\frac{nH}{4}\delta_n^2}\sqrt{n}}IA​(n)IB​(n)​≤ce−4nH​δn2​n​

Hence we want nδn2log⁡n→∞\dfrac{n\delta_n^2}{\log n} \to \inftylognnδn2​​→∞.

In fact, from all the conditions, and letting δn=n−a\delta_n = n^{-a}δn​=n−a (power scaling, natural), we get a∈(13,12)a \in (\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{2})a∈(31​,21​). I will keep the choice a=25a = \frac{2}{5}a=52​. This allows all the control conditions to work, and the same control is used in the multidimensional case as well. It is important to note it now, as I will simply use this control right from the start and it will all magically work out, but the point is that the interval is forced and all the choices there will work, and it is not really magical.

Estimating the Partition Function¶

We will now estimate the asymptotics of the normalized partition function. We will be considering the regular case with compact parameter space WWW in a Euclidean space Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd.

Zn(0)=∫e−nKn(w)φ(w)dwZ_n^{(0)} = \int e^{-nK_n(w)}\varphi(w)dwZn(0)​=∫e−nKn​(w)φ(w)dw
(18)

The issue is that we cannot directly Taylor expand this. h(w)−h(w0)≥0h(w) - h(w_0) \geq 0h(w)−h(w0​)≥0, but it need not be true Kn(w)−Kn(w0)≥0K_n(w) - K_n(w_0) \geq 0Kn​(w)−Kn​(w0​)≥0. Hence, something else needs to be done. We need to decompose our function of a distance like function and a fluctuation around that and hope it behaves nicely. But why should we expect that? The fluctuation can have a very weird distribution after all. The central limit theorem comes to the rescue in controlling that, it says that the fluctuation is bounded in large samples. This is the universality principle at rescue, which says that you should expect the fluctuation of f(X1,...,Xn)f(X_1, ..., X_n)f(X1​,...,Xn​) to be bounded if the variables are weakly dependent and fff sufficiently smooth.

So we define the empirical process

ξn(w)=n(Kn(w)−K(w))\xi_n(w) = \sqrt{n}(K_n(w) - K(w))ξn​(w)=n​(Kn​(w)−K(w))
(19)

This centres the expectation (it is now 0) and by the multidimensional central limit theorem, this converges in distribution to the Gaussian distribution, hence it is Op(1)O_p(1)Op​(1),

We divide our partition function into an integral around a neighborhood (we call that the essential part) and the complement of that (called the non essential part). We will see that decomposition into this process works in trying to estimate the essential part, and in figuring out the non essential part, we will need to modify it more. There, we will perform a simple instance of Hironaka Resolution Theorem. It is important to grasp that idea and why it comes in the first place. We will see what that is about when we get there.

Essential Part¶

We have

nKn(w)=nξn(w)+nK(w)nK_n(w) = \sqrt{n}\xi_n(w) + nK(w)nKn​(w)=n​ξn​(w)+nK(w)
(20)

We will Taylor expand both terms with Lagrange remainder. I am going to remove terms directly which are 0, you can check that. Call the Hessian of KKK at w0w_0w0​ as JJJ.

nK(w)=n2ΔtJΔ+n6∇3K(c)[Δ,Δ,Δ]nK(w) = \frac{n}{2}\Delta^tJ\Delta + \frac{n}{6}\nabla^3K(c)[\Delta, \Delta, \Delta]nK(w)=2n​ΔtJΔ+6n​∇3K(c)[Δ,Δ,Δ]
(21)

The first term is A1A_1A1​ the second term is A2A_2A2​.

nξn(w)=nΔt∇ξn(w0)+n2Δt∇2ξn(w0)Δ+n6∇3ξn(c)[Δ,Δ,Δ]\sqrt{n}\xi_n(w) = \sqrt{n}\Delta^t\nabla\xi_n(w_0) + \frac{\sqrt{n}}{2}\Delta^t\nabla^2\xi_n(w_0)\Delta + \frac{\sqrt{n}}{6}\nabla^3\xi_n(c)[\Delta, \Delta, \Delta]n​ξn​(w)=n​Δt∇ξn​(w0​)+2n​​Δt∇2ξn​(w0​)Δ+6n​​∇3ξn​(c)[Δ,Δ,Δ]
(22)

The first term, second term, and the third term are A3,A4,A5A_3, A_4, A_5A3​,A4​,A5​ respectively.

We want to discard all the op(1)o_p(1)op​(1) terms into our remainder function Rn(w)R_n(w)Rn​(w) for sandwiching.

Let us look at A2A_2A2​ first.

A2  ≤M2nδn3A_2 \;\leq M_2n\delta_n^3A2​≤M2​nδn3​
(23)

Our choice of δn\delta_nδn​ is predecided, δn=n−2/5\delta_n = n^{-2/5}δn​=n−2/5, so we see that A2→0A_2 \to 0A2​→0. We can safely push this into our remainder.

Now, A4A_4A4​ is a random variable. Let XnX_nXn​ be the norm of the Hessian, which is a random variable. Observe that {Xn}=Op(1)\{X_n\} = O_p(1){Xn​}=Op​(1)

A4≤M4anXnan=nδn2A_4 \leq M_4 a_nX_n \qquad a_n = \sqrt{n}\delta_n^2A4​≤M4​an​Xn​an​=n​δn2​
(24)

Since an→0a_n \to 0an​→0, {Xn}=Op(1)\{X_n\} = O_p(1){Xn​}=Op​(1), we have {anXn}=op(1)\{a_nX_n\} = o_p(1){an​Xn​}=op​(1).

Hence A4A_4A4​ is op(1)o_p(1)op​(1), and similarly, so is A5A_5A5​.

Hence we write

nKn(w)=A1+A3+Rn(w)Rn(w)=op(1)nK_n(w) = A_1 + A_3 + R_n(w) \qquad R_n(w) = o_p(1)nKn​(w)=A1​+A3​+Rn​(w)Rn​(w)=op​(1)
(25)

We will sandwich and estimate the same way we did for the one dimensional Laplace integral. Assume all sufficient smoothness for the bounds. Let ∣Rn∣≤ρn|R_n| \leq \rho_n∣Rn​∣≤ρn​ where ρn→0\rho_n \to 0ρn​→0 in probability. Then we have

e−ρn(φ(w0)−aδn)∫e−A1−A3dw≤Zn(1)≤eρn(φ(w0)+aδn)∫e−A1−A3dwe^{-\rho_n}(\varphi(w_0) - a\delta_n)\int e^{-A_1 - A_3}dw \leq Z_n^{(1)} \leq e^{\rho_n}(\varphi(w_0) + a \delta_n)\int e^{-A_1 - A_3}dwe−ρn​(φ(w0​)−aδn​)∫e−A1​−A3​dw≤Zn(1)​≤eρn​(φ(w0​)+aδn​)∫e−A1​−A3​dw
(26)

Now all that is left to do is to compute the integral

Gn=∫e−A1−A3dwG_n = \int e^{-A_1 - A_3}dwGn​=∫e−A1​−A3​dw
(27)

The idea is to complete the square, write the sum of quadratic + linear as a quadratic + constant. And we know how to handle the quadratic for the exponential, and the constant gets handled trivially.

One can write

n2ΔtJΔ+nΔt∇ξn(w0)=12∣∣J1/2u−ζn∣∣2−12∣∣ζn∣∣2\frac{n}{2}\Delta^tJ\Delta + \sqrt{n}\Delta^t\nabla\xi_n(w_0) = \frac{1}{2}||J^{1/2}u - \zeta_n||^2 - \frac{1}{2}||\zeta_n||^22n​ΔtJΔ+n​Δt∇ξn​(w0​)=21​∣∣J1/2u−ζn​∣∣2−21​∣∣ζn​∣∣2

where u=n(w−w0)u = \sqrt{n}(w - w_0)u=n​(w−w0​) and ζn=−J−1/2bn\zeta_n = -J^{-1/2}b_nζn​=−J−1/2bn​ and bn=∇ξn(w0)b_n = \nabla \xi_n(w_0)bn​=∇ξn​(w0​).

We first do the change of coordinates from www to w−w0w - w_0w−w0​ which does not change the integral as it is just a translation, then from w−w0w - w_0w−w0​ to n(w−w0)\sqrt{n}(w - w_0)n​(w−w0​) which gives the factor (1n)d(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}})^d(n​1​)d (this is just the determinant of the transition from the latter to the former).

Now the final transition from uuu to v=J1/2u−ζnv = J^{1/2}u - \zeta_nv=J1/2u−ζn​ gives the factor det⁡(J)−1/2\det(J)^{-1/2}det(J)−1/2

Hence,

Gn=n−d/2det⁡(J)−1/2e∣∣ζn∣∣2/2∫Dne−∣∣v∣∣2/2dvG_n = n^{-d/2}\det(J)^{-1/2}e^{||\zeta_n||^2/2} \int_{D_n} e^{-||v||^2/2}dvGn​=n−d/2det(J)−1/2e∣∣ζn​∣∣2/2∫Dn​​e−∣∣v∣∣2/2dv

where DnD_nDn​ is some ellipsoid. But this is contained in a ball centred around −ζn-\zeta_n−ζn​, and it also contains a ball around −ζn-\zeta_n−ζn​, and both of them tend to the entire Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞, in probability. Zn(1)∼(2π)d/2φ(w0)n−d/2det⁡(J)−1/2e∣∣ζn∣∣2/2Z_n^{(1)} \sim (2\pi)^{d/2}\varphi(w_0)n^{-d/2}\det(J)^{-1/2}e^{||\zeta_n||^2/2}Zn(1)​∼(2π)d/2φ(w0​)n−d/2det(J)−1/2e∣∣ζn​∣∣2/2
(30)

Now we deal with the non essential part.

Non Essential Part¶

Now we need to lower bound nKn(w)nK_n(w)nKn​(w). Well, we can bound nK(w)nK(w)nK(w), but how do we go about nξn(w)\sqrt{n}\xi_n(w)n​ξn​(w)? We cannot actually do this, since this fluctuation is Op(n)O_p(\sqrt{n})Op​(n​). We will need to do some sort of normalization here.

Let us first deal with nK(w)nK(w)nK(w) though. We will do it the same way we did the one-dimensional case. The only thing that changes is that this is multidimensional, so the min of the second order term is 12λmin(J)δn2\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{min}(J)\delta_n^221​λmin​(J)δn2​, so we get the lower bound this time as nK(w)≥14λminnδn2nK(w) \geq \frac{1}{4}\lambda_{min}n\delta_n^2nK(w)≥41​λmin​nδn2​. Feel free to do the argument again formally here as an exercise.

Let us deal with the fluctuation. As discovered, we will need to normalize this, where the normalization factor has to be of order n\sqrt{n}n​ with respect to K(w)K(w)K(w).

Define the process

γn(w)=ξn(w)K(w)=n(Kn(w)−K(w))K(w)\gamma_n(w) = \frac{\xi_n(w)}{\sqrt{K(w)}} = \frac{\sqrt{n}(K_n(w) - K(w))}{\sqrt{K(w)}}γn​(w)=K(w)​ξn​(w)​=K(w)​n​(Kn​(w)−K(w))​
(31)

Claim: γn(w)=Op(1)\gamma_n(w) = O_p(1)γn​(w)=Op​(1)

Proof: Since the model is regular, relatively finite variance holds for the log density ratio function: EX[f(X,w)2]≤c0K(w)E_X[f(X, w)^2] \leq c_0 K(w)EX​[f(X,w)2]≤c0​K(w) for all www.

Now,

V[γn(w)]=V[ξn(w)]K(w)=VX[f(X,w)]K(w)≤EX[f(X,w)2]K(w)≤c0V[\gamma_n(w)] = \frac{V[\xi_n(w)]}{K(w)} = \frac{V_X[f(X, w)]}{K(w)} \leq \frac{E_X[f(X, w)^2]}{K(w)} \leq c_0V[γn​(w)]=K(w)V[ξn​(w)]​=K(w)VX​[f(X,w)]​≤K(w)EX​[f(X,w)2]​≤c0​
(32)

Hence,

P(∣γn(w)∣>t)≤c0t2  ⟹  γn(w)=Op(1)P(|\gamma_n(w)| > t) \leq \frac{c_0}{t^2} \implies \gamma_n(w) = O_p(1)P(∣γn​(w)∣>t)≤t2c0​​⟹γn​(w)=Op​(1)
(33)

Note that we were able to get this from relatively finite variance, which we got since the model was regular. When we move to the more general case, we will simply need to take this as an assumption, and I am not sure why we should assume this to be true. But it will still be a great improvement.

There are two issues with the definition above though:

  1. In a more general model, W0W_0W0​ is not one point, it is a real analytic set. Hence f(x,w)f(x, w)f(x,w) cannot be treated locally. More precisely, what this means is that the Taylor expansion we have been doing does not work directly, since now the Hessian is degenerate (not positive definite) (this is a heuristic argument). So this definition of the process does not really work anymore. Keep this in mind, we will deal with this formally later.

  2. The second is the fact that the process is not defined at W0W_0W0​ as the denominator is 0. It may not even be possible to continuously extend our process to W0W_0W0​.

The second issue holds even for our regular model. What is the “resolution” here? The solution is to perform a diffeomorphism of the space, and then extend the function to w0w_0w0​ there. This is the main idea one should keep in mind. We describe the solution formally now.

Define a diffeomorphism from Rd\0\mathbb{R}^d \backslash 0Rd\0 to (0,∞)×Sd−1(0, \infty) \times S^{d-1}(0,∞)×Sd−1 that takes w−w0→rθw - w_0 \to r\thetaw−w0​→rθ where r=∣∣w−w0∣∣r = ||w - w_0||r=∣∣w−w0​∣∣ and θ=w−w0∣∣w−w0∣∣\theta = \dfrac{w - w_0}{||w - w_0||}θ=∣∣w−w0​∣∣w−w0​​. The numerator becomes rbn⋅θ+O(r2)rb_n\cdot\theta + O(r^2)rbn​⋅θ+O(r2) and K=rθtJθ/2(1+O(r))\sqrt{K} = r\sqrt{\theta^tJ\theta/2(1 + O(r))}K​=rθtJθ/2(1+O(r))​. One can check that the limit now exists.

This is the simplest instance of the Resolution, and the more general case is handled by Hironaka’s Resolution Theorem, which deals with both the issues mentioned above.

By using the inequality ∣ab∣≤a2+b22|ab| \leq \dfrac{a^2 + b^2}{2}∣ab∣≤2a2+b2​, we get (take a=nK,b=γna = \sqrt{nK}, b = \gamma_na=nK​,b=γn​)

12nK(w)−12Γn2≤nKn(w)≤32nK(w)+12Γn2\frac{1}{2}nK(w) - \frac{1}{2}\Gamma_n^2 \leq nK_n(w) \leq \frac{3}{2}nK(w) + \frac{1}{2}\Gamma_n^221​nK(w)−21​Γn2​≤nKn​(w)≤23​nK(w)+21​Γn2​
(34)

where Γn2=sup⁡w∈W∣∣γn(w)∣∣2\Gamma_n^2 = \sup_{w \in W} ||\gamma_n(w)||^2Γn2​=supw∈W​∣∣γn​(w)∣∣2. Observe that even if Xn=Op(1)X_n = O_p(1)Xn​=Op​(1), sup⁡Xn\sup X_nsupXn​ need not be Op(1)O_p(1)Op​(1). Hence, this is an added assumption that Γn=Op(1)\Gamma_n = O_p(1)Γn​=Op​(1). Also, the existence of Γn\Gamma_nΓn​ comes from the fact that γn(w)\gamma_n(w)γn​(w) is a continuous function (we have extended it continuously) on a compact space.

This finally enables us to sandwich the non essential part of the partition function.

Using the lower bound nKn(w)≥12nK(w)−12Γn2nK_n(w) \geq \frac{1}{2}nK(w) - \frac{1}{2}\Gamma_n^2nKn​(w)≥21​nK(w)−21​Γn2​, together with nK(w)≥14λminnδn2nK(w) \geq \frac{1}{4}\lambda_{min}n\delta_n^2nK(w)≥41​λmin​nδn2​ on BBB, we get

Zn(2)≤eΓn2/2∫Bexp⁡(−12nK(w))φ(w)dw≤eΓn2/2exp⁡(−18λminnδn2)∫Bφ(w)dwZ_n^{(2)} \leq e^{\Gamma_n^2/2}\int_B \exp(-\frac{1}{2}nK(w))\varphi(w)dw \leq e^{\Gamma_n^2/2}\exp(-\frac{1}{8}\lambda_{min}n\delta_n^2)\int_B\varphi(w)dwZn(2)​≤eΓn2​/2∫B​exp(−21​nK(w))φ(w)dw≤eΓn2​/2exp(−81​λmin​nδn2​)∫B​φ(w)dw
(35)

Now, since φ(w)\varphi(w)φ(w) is a density function, the integral over BBB is less than equal to 1.

Zn(2)≤eΓn2/2exp⁡(−18λminnδn2)Z_n^{(2)} \leq e^{\Gamma_n^2/2}\exp(-\frac{1}{8}\lambda_{min}n\delta_n^2)Zn(2)​≤eΓn2​/2exp(−81​λmin​nδn2​)
(36)

Since Γn=Op(1)\Gamma_n = O_p(1)Γn​=Op​(1), the factor eΓn2/2e^{\Gamma_n^2/2}eΓn2​/2 is Op(1)O_p(1)Op​(1), and it does not affect the conclusions below. This directly gives the following two results, the second one being what we need to show:

nkZn(2)→0 in probability for every kn^kZ_n^{(2)} \to 0 \quad \text{ in probability for every k}nkZn(2)​→0 in probability for every k

Zn(2)Zn(1)→0\dfrac{Z_n^{(2)}}{Z_n^{(1)}} \to 0Zn(1)​Zn(2)​​→0

Hence the non essential part is negligible, and we have estimated the essential part of the partition function. We are done here.

We get the asymptotic expansion of the free energy in the regular case now.

Fn=nLn(w0)+Fn(0)Fn(0)=−log⁡Zn(0)=−log⁡Zn(1)(1+Zn(2)Zn(1))=−log⁡Zn(1)+op(1)F_n = nL_n(w_0) + F_n^{(0)} \qquad F_n^{(0)} = -\log Z_n^{(0)} = -\log Z_n^{(1)}(1 + \frac{Z_n^{(2)}}{Z_n^{(1)}}) = -\log Z_n^{(1)} + o_p(1)Fn​=nLn​(w0​)+Fn(0)​Fn(0)​=−logZn(0)​=−logZn(1)​(1+Zn(1)​Zn(2)​​)=−logZn(1)​+op​(1)

Fn=nLn(w0)+d2log⁡n−d2log⁡(2π)+12log⁡(det⁡J)−log⁡φ(w0)−∣∣ζn∣∣22+op(1)F_n = nL_n(w_0) + \frac{d}{2}\log n - \frac{d}{2}\log (2\pi) + \frac{1}{2}\log (\det J) - \log\varphi(w_0) - \frac{||\zeta_n||^2}{2} + o_p(1)Fn​=nLn​(w0​)+2d​logn−2d​log(2π)+21​log(detJ)−logφ(w0​)−2∣∣ζn​∣∣2​+op​(1)

Checking the losses on the sine model¶

Let us check if the theory actually works. We are dealing with the sine regression problem here. The figures are generated by Opus 5.5.

We now check the non realizable case. The best parameter is still w0=(0.3,1.2)w_0 = (0.3, 1.2)w0​=(0.3,1.2), but now I=σ2JI = \sigma^2 JI=σ2J, so tr(IJ−1)=4.5≠d\mathrm{tr}(IJ^{-1}) = 4.5 \neq dtr(IJ−1)=4.5=d.

Exercise: I am not going to prove uniform integrability (UI), as the argument does not seem sufficiently instructive and reusable. Assume it and derive the asymptotes of the expectations of the observables.

Point Estimators¶

There are other statistical estimation methods when the true distribution is regular for the statistical model, that are not entirely Bayesian in nature.

wML=arg max⁡w∈W∏i=1np(xi∣w)Maximum LikelihoodwMAP=arg max⁡w∈Wφ(w)∏i=1np(xi∣w)Maximum A PosterioriwPM=Ew[w]Posterior Mean Estimator\begin{aligned} w_{ML} &= \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{w \in W} \prod_{i=1}^np(x_i|w) && \text{Maximum Likelihood} \\ w_{MAP} &= \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{w \in W}\varphi(w)\prod_{i = 1}^np(x_i|w) && \text{Maximum A Posteriori} \\ w_{PM} &= E_w[w] && \text{Posterior Mean Estimator} \end{aligned}wML​wMAP​wPM​​=w∈Wargmax​i=1∏n​p(xi​∣w)=w∈Wargmax​φ(w)i=1∏n​p(xi​∣w)=Ew​[w]​​Maximum LikelihoodMaximum A PosterioriPosterior Mean Estimator​
(63)

Remember the completion of the square that we did for nKnnK_nnKn​. The minimizer, which is wMLw_{ML}wML​ satisfies w≈w0+J−1/2ζnnw \approx w_0 + \frac{J^{-1/2}\zeta_n}{\sqrt{n}}w≈w0​+n​J−1/2ζn​​.

More precisely (prove this yourself),

wML=w0+J−1/2ζnn+op(1n)w_{ML} = w_0 + \frac{J^{-1/2}\zeta_n}{\sqrt{n}} + o_p(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}})wML​=w0​+n​J−1/2ζn​​+op​(n​1​)
(64)

and the other two estimators also have the same expansion up to this order.

Definition: The generalization and training losses of the maximum likelihood method are defined by

Gn(ML)=L(wML)Tn(ML)=Ln(wML)\begin{aligned} G_n(ML) &= L(w_{ML}) \\ T_n(ML) &= L_n(w_{ML}) \end{aligned}Gn​(ML)Tn​(ML)​=L(wML​)=Ln​(wML​)​
(65)

We can now find the asymptotes by just the same standard method.

Gn(ML)=L(w0)+∣∣ζn∣∣22n+op(1n)Tn(ML)=Ln(w0)−∣∣ζn∣∣22n+op(1n)\begin{aligned} G_n(ML) &= L(w_0) + \frac{||\zeta_n||^2}{2n} + o_p(\frac{1}{n}) \\ T_n(ML) &= L_n(w_0) - \frac{||\zeta_n||^2}{2n} + o_p(\frac{1}{n}) \end{aligned}Gn​(ML)Tn​(ML)​=L(w0​)+2n∣∣ζn​∣∣2​+op​(n1​)=Ln​(w0​)−2n∣∣ζn​∣∣2​+op​(n1​)​
(66)
